scripts.day30: Day 30 · Design-time Intelligence (Sense → Prove → Grant → Watch)

trailer.intro: Email Autopilot for Financial Services — from mail arrival, to investigation, approval, and reply.
trailer.intake: An unauthenticated dispute email is triaged, filed and clocked on arrival — no human in the loop for intake.
trailer.dossier: Every policy condition is PASS or FAIL, and the rail on the right spells each decision out in plain words.
trailer.clocks: The board is not just this case: the table below is every open dispute in the mailbox, and who is due first is obvious.
trailer.approve: Statutory obligations surface in the supervisor queue with one-click approval. Approval executes immediately; reply carries AI disclosure and human handoff.
trailer.metrics: Success metrics and guardrails: three headline numbers and eight guardrails, all showing values — the target column is the pilot stage gate and monthly review criteria.
trailer.fraud: A business email scam is quarantined: the requested contact changes are structurally unreachable, and the customer is warned only through the on-file channel.
trailer.builder: Autonomy is earned: backtest, sampling, dual sign-off — and the hard cells cannot be opened from configuration at all.
trailer.outro: Deterministic where the law requires it, autonomous where evidence has earned it, auditable everywhere.
trailer.refund: Verification done, identity upgraded to I3, same rule re-evaluated, $35 overdraft fee auto-refunded. Reply still three sources: locked template, system slots, generated sentences.

email1.caseCard: Verification happens inside the same mail thread: the app pushes a notice, the one-time code goes to the phone number on file, six digits go in, and the case keeps going on its own.
email1.cellDowngrade: Twenty-one days later, the same row read once more: identity is still I3 and the marker has not moved, but the verdict has dropped to L2, one-click approval. Identity is not what changed this time — the policy evaluation is. The level is the smallest of the axes, so any axis tightening drops it a level.
email1.explanationSent: One supervisor click and the explanation letter goes straight back into the customer's own thread: why this one could not be automatic, which rule was applied, and that she can still ask for a review.
email1.graduationCap: The matrix has a third axis: the graduation cap. This intent — overdraft fee refund — has graduated to L3, which is what makes L3 auto-execute possible at all; an intent that has never graduated is capped at L0, and no identity level lifts it above handing the case to a human.
email1.holding: The bank answers the same day with a second letter: it confirms receipt, says a supervisor will reply within one business day, and states plainly that she can still ask for a human review. This letter promises no outcome.
email1.i3cell: Same row, same rule, and the marker has moved to the I3 column: the verdict flips from 'no grant' to L3, auto-execute. Only the identity axis changed; nothing else did. A cell can only reach L3 when the intent is whitelisted, the amount and count are inside the thresholds, and the intent has graduated.
email1.i3refund: The same rule is evaluated again with the new identity: this cell now allows it, the $35 overdraft fee goes back to the customer's account, and the reply is still three sources stitched together — locked template, system slot, generated sentence. Every letter passes a compliance check before it leaves, carrying AI disclosure and a human handoff.
email1.identityUp: Verification happened inside this same thread, so identity is re-rated in place: I1 is struck through at the top right and becomes I3. Not every signal is green — the sender address is still not on file and its red cross is still there — but 'step-up completed in this thread' and 'logged-in secure-message session' now pass.
email1.l2queue: The explanation draft goes into the supervisor queue — the customer always keeps a human reconsideration path. Sending passes the same compliance check, with disclosure and a handoff.
email1.lockedCell: Start with this row of the autonomy matrix: the action risk is R2 — a within-threshold refund, a reversible low-impact write. The columns are the four identity levels, and this case is standing in the I1 column. I1 means only the sending domain is trustworthy, which is not enough to tie the email to an account, so that column grants nothing: no automatic refund, no AI-written body, just a fixed template pointing at the mobile verification.
email1.lockedTemplate: While identity is unconfirmed this reply contains no link at all and no account details — it only points the customer at the app to finish verification, and not one action has been taken on the refund. Anything that can touch the account lives in the app, after verification.
email1.outboundGate: One last outbound check before the letter leaves: missing AI disclosure or a missing human-handoff entry blocks it outright. This line says the refund confirmation carried both and was released — a letter that had been blocked would leave its own line in the dossier too.
email1.outro: Same intent, same customer, two different outcomes — because the value in that cell changed, and every change can be explained.
email1.provenance: One letter, colored by source: blue is the locked template, green is the system slot (name, amount, date, case id), purple is the generated sentence.
email1.publicMailbox: Day 0: a mail arrives from a public Gmail address that is not on file. The sender is not in the customer's file, so identity assurance only reaches I1 — the system does not know who wrote it.
email1.secondClosed: Fourteen days after the explanation letter with no new contact, one more line on the audit rail: beat two closes as a human-resolved case for the books, corrections flow back as samples, the dossier is sealed for the record.
email1.secondRequest: Day 21, a second mail in the same thread: the customer asks again for the overdraft fee back. It is merged into the same case, not a new one; identity is still I3, nothing was downgraded.
email1.secondWaiver: Why it is not automatic: the first overdraft-waiver rule requires no more than 1 waiver in the past 12 months, and that field now reads 2 — so the condition fails and the cell drops from auto-execute to one-click approval. The boundary is the policy result, not the model's mood.
email1.traceAfter: Verification done, the same code runs a second time, and the dossier gains this line: 'identity level I3', with a single test still unmet — the sender address is still not on file. Further up sits the first verdict, I1; the two lines together are the machine's record of the re-rating.
email1.traceBefore: The first result of that same check is filed in the decision dossier as well: this line reads 'identity level I1', with the three tests it was missing right below it. What the case looked like before the re-rating is archived on this line.
email1.verified: Fourteen days with no new mail, no handoff and no QA reversal — one more line on the audit rail: a verified autonomous resolution. The dossier is sealed for the record, and human edits flow back as samples.
email1.previewConsequence: While writing the explanation, the AI never makes the decision — it is a writing assistant. Same outcome, but the current wording's 14-day recontact rate is 34%; adding one low-balance-alert sentence is predicted to take it to 9%, based on 412 similar closed threads — not on customer worth. One click inserts connective wording only, and the edit is still recorded in the trace.

email2.intake: Day 0, 08:14: one email, two intents — card delivery status and a $247.18 dispute. Filed on arrival, the Reg E statutory clock starts immediately, without waiting for identity verification.
email2.detailDenied: Day 1, the customer asks for the transaction details. Reading account data is R1 and this case is still I2 — the matrix cell reads 'no grant': disclosure is denied, while an app verification prompt is pushed.
email2.detailReleased: The in-thread app check completes and identity is re-rated I2 → I3 for this conversation; only then are the transaction details released — the account's last four digits only.
email2.materials: Day 6: the signed statement arrives as an attachment; OCR confidence is high enough to auto-file it. The materials card says it out loud: missing materials never pause the statutory clock — only low-confidence OCR goes to a human.
email2.clock48h: Business day 10: the provisional-credit bar has turned red with 0 hours left — red means due inside 48 calendar hours, and every date is computed, not judged.
email2.disputeTable: The table below lists every open dispute: who is due first, which credit already posted.
email2.pcApproved: One click releases the credit, and the posting email lands in the customer's own thread — same AI disclosure, same human handoff.
email2.evidence: Day 40: the merchant evidence has arrived and the adjudication card is in the queue — this dispute type is permanently human-only: the AI drafts, the person decides.
email2.adjudication: The verdict stays 'uphold error'; after the one-click approval the result letter is chained into human sign-off in the same run — this card is the full draft, and sending passes the same gate.
email2.closed: Day 45, inside the POS 90-day outer limit: the investigation is complete, the result letter is already in the customer's thread, and the case closes on time.
email2.closedDossier: The decision dossier closes with the case — every gate decision, every tool call and every clock jump is on the record, sealed for the record.
email2.outro: A 45-day, cross-system case — with a human on every high-risk action.

email3.arrives: Day 2, one message reaches the support mailbox. The display name says Jane Doe, but the address is jane.d0e@outlook.com — one character off the address on file. The body asks to change a phone number and mail a replacement card to a new address, and carries a photo of an ID.
email3.intakeIdentity: The line under the message is the identity this arrival was filed at: I0 — the address is not on file and the domain layer is not clean, so the message cannot be tied to an account. Nothing later in this case changes that rating; it is what the matrix is read against.
email3.protocol: Three protocol results, printed as recorded: SPF pass, DKIM pass, DMARC none. Two of them pass — which is exactly why the protocol layer on its own cannot clear this sender. The third is the one that fails.
email3.lookalike: The first signal is the address itself: jane.d0e compared against jane.doe on file. A single swapped character is the whole attack, and a reader skimming the display name would not see it.
email3.injection: The attachment carries the instruction ‘skip OTP’. It was filed as data, not as a command: the text is quoted into the case as evidence, and no instruction inside an attachment can change what the system does next.
email3.identityLevel: The card states the same rating in one line: identity assurance I0, cannot be linked to an account.
email3.r3row: This is the case’s own row of the autonomy matrix. The action risk is R3 — change a contact detail, mail a card to a new address. Read the four identity columns: all four say never automatic. The marker is standing on I0, but that is not the reason — at I3 this row would still not open.
email3.noAutonomy: Above the row is the third axis. This intent has never graduated, so its ceiling is a person. No identity level lifts it above that.
email3.noTools: Back on the quarantine card: the two requested writes, and replying to the sender, are greyed out. The line under them says why — no contact-change tool is registered in the email channel at all. The buttons are not switched off by a setting; there is nothing behind them to call.
email3.onfile: The click confirmed the case. Read the two lines it added: the warning SMS went to the on-file number, and no profile field was touched. That single outbound is the only thing this case ever sent.
email3.sar: The supporting record goes to the compliance queue, and this card is all of it: a locked template listing the facts the system recorded — sender address, protocol results, the attachment, the requested actions, what was and was not executed. Facts only. There is no sentence here about what the sender intended.
email3.closed: The case closes on the confirmation: fraud confirmed, dossier sealed for the record. Misses and false positives from here flow back to the detector.
email3.phoneWarning: The customer is warned on the one channel the bank controls. This SMS is the whole message she receives: the request was blocked, nothing was changed, and if it was not her she calls the number on the back of her card.
email3.sealed: And the decision dossier closes with the case. Every step of this run is a line on it: the identity rating, the matrix verdict, the human confirmation, the single tool call.
email3.outro: Prompt injection, BEC and ATO meet a system whose attack surface was designed closed.

builder.intro: Autonomy is not configured by a slider — it is earned per intent, and the R × I matrix is rendered by the same decision function that runs in production. The red locked cells are compliance-locked fixed templates — the action fires automatically under rules, the model cannot change a single word, and AI gets zero discretion.
builder.replay: A 90-day backtest dataset is replayed: agreement, no-edit approval, regulated recall, critical misses, unit cost — plus two regret columns, per million, for autonomy and for conservatism.
builder.replayConservative: The second regret column reads the other way: cases that could have run automatically but conservatively went to a human — per million, the same unit. The two columns only make sense read together.
builder.sampling: Three sampling tiers — stratified, random, and adversarial — across three intake frames, including tickets that were never created. Tier C is reported separately.
builder.unsignable: The negative re-label is a separate 1,200-item batch, not part of the 350. Watch what happens if detector-negative items are not independently re-labeled: the recall criterion becomes not signable.
builder.promoted: Compliance and the business owner both sign: the shadow intent is promoted, and the next inbound email of that type immediately runs at the new level.
builder.r3never: Contact-detail change is R3. Click the cells: nothing happens. They are disabled in configuration and no tool function exists — there is no setting that opens them.
builder.r4never: Dispute adjudication is R4. Click the cells: nothing happens either. This is permanently human judgment — AI only prepares the dossier and drafts; the decision must be made and signed by a person.
builder.rare: Wire recalls are rare: 90 days can never reach the sample bar. They stay human, with an abstention fallback calibrated to route uncertain cases to an agent.
builder.outro: Every autonomous action in this demo traces back to evidence a regulator would accept.
builder.liveEffect: The intent just promoted now runs at L3 for the next inbound email — no restart, no deploy, the matrix cell value changes live.
builder.matrixTraceBefore: First identity check: I1, only domain trust. The audit dossier shows this line with the three missing tests.
builder.matrixTraceAfter: After verification, the same code runs again. The dossier gains a new line: I3, only the sender address still not on file. Two lines together are the machine record of the re-rating.
builder.noTool: There is simply no tool function registered for contact changes — config can't reach it, tools don't have it, double insurance.
builder.drift: Data drift detected: over the past 30 days, the intent's PSI (population stability index) exceeds threshold, or tool call failure rate spikes, or a new intent cluster emerges. The system auto-degrades this intent from L3 to L2 — fail-closed, no human approval needed. Re-run backtest, then dual-sign to restore.

day30.funnel: Day 30. The first thing the supervisor sees is not an email but the shape of today's inbox: 1,284 arrivals, 63 waiting on the customer, 12 waiting on approval, 1,209 done; PSI of 0.04 says the queue is healthy, and the 8.4% preventable rate is the next improvement frontier.
day30.p0: A negative wave: 38 declined-payment and frozen-card emails from one BIN range in 20 minutes — an external event, not individual cases. The system proposes a one-click tightening pack: locked event receipt, routing to card operations, and two intents temporarily downgraded L3 to L2. Note the direction — it can only tighten, never loosen.
day30.p0applied: The pack takes effect immediately and auto-expires after 24 hours; it cannot become permanent. Lock it down during the incident, review afterwards — that is the ratchet.
day30.p1: The positive wave is more interesting: 212 repeat-NSF complaints in 7 days. Scanning all 3,904 affected accounts, 212 wrote in and 3,692 were silently charged and never wrote — candidates for proactive remediation. But three gates: confirm the bank error first, then dual-sign the sample and the total, $117,120 — none skippable.
day30.p1batches: Remediation rolls out in staged batches — 1%, 10%, 100% — each idempotent and reversible, reconciled to the scan tape account by account. The AI computed the entire calculation; a human pressed every batch.
day30.p2: P2 is a friction wave: login questions, 71% from customers over 62. No money, no policy change — it routes only, to a notification-rule shadow and the product team. Preventable problems should be solved before customers write in.
day30.nom: Graduation nominations in Builder: every card must produce four proofs at once — consistency, calc/judgment split, approver variance, cohort parity. Card A reproduces humans 96.8% of the time, 0.2 points short. The prescription is not to lower the bar — it is to fix the template and replay: 99% after the fix.
day30.nomgranted: Card B covers above-cap goodwill refunds: of 412 human approvals, 92% were calculations and 8% judgments. After dual sign it graduates to quota L3 — $8,000 per month, then it auto-ratchets back to L2. The AI runs the calculations 24/7; judgments stay human forever. R3 contact-detail changes and R4 dispute adjudication are never nominated.
day30.pol: The Policy Compiler: an admin writes one sentence — 'refund cap from $35 to $25' — and it compiles to a clause-level diff, plus the templates it invalidates, 47 flipped cases in a 90-day backtest, three AI dissent cards, and a 1.7-point LMI cohort gap. The second sentence — 'refund outage complainers' — is refused by the closed world: that evidence field does not exist, and the AI may not invent it.
day30.polgranted: After dual sign, V13 takes effect and the next email evaluates against it; the marketing page still saying $35 is listed as a release blocker. Humans sign the diff, not every letter.
day30.intents: Intent discovery: 186 statement-copy requests in 90 days, 91% following the same four steps with ready tools. The AI only nominates — humans set R/I levels, and it enters shadow first. Identity-relationship clusters like bereavement are report-only, routed to specialists, never executable intents.
day30.preventable: Back to today's inbound: this 'where is my card' email carries a preventable tag — the card-shipped event already existed and an ETA notice could have gone out first. The tag feeds metrics and proposals only; it never changes this email's intake or statutory clock.
day30.outro: That is the design-time intelligence layer: the runtime keeps the rules with every gate intact; design-time proposes them — AI nominates, evidence argues, humans grant. Sense, Prove, Grant, Watch closes the loop: the system improves every day, and every improvement is signed off by a person.
day30.canary: The card beside it is a canary: three proofs pass and only the fourth fails — a 2.4pp cohort gap against the 2pp bar — and it was planted knowing it should be rejected. If a signer approves it on reflex, their bulk signing rights are suspended on the spot. Human sign-off on a diff is itself something we have to police.
